July: Peak Season Riding

July is high summer in Britain — the warmest month on average, school holidays begin, and the tourism industry hits full swing. For motorcycle touring, July offers the most reliable weather but the busiest roads. The trick is knowing when and where to ride.

Conditions

  • Temperature: Average 14-23°C. Heatwaves can bring 30°C+ in southern England. Scotland stays cooler at 14-20°C.
  • Daylight: Still over 16 hours. Plenty of time for long touring days.
  • Weather: The most reliably dry month, but thunderstorms can develop on hot afternoons. The west is wetter than the east.

Beating the Crowds

  • Ride early: Before 9am, even popular roads are quiet. The first two hours of a July day are golden.
  • Ride midweek: Weekend traffic in tourist areas can be three times the midweek volume.
  • Choose less obvious destinations: While everyone heads to the Lake District and Snowdonia, the North Pennines, Scottish Borders, and mid-Wales offer comparable scenery with a fraction of the traffic.
  • Use B-roads: Tourist traffic sticks to A-roads. Parallel B-roads are often empty and more enjoyable.

Hot Weather Riding

Riding in genuine heat requires adjustment:

  • Stay hydrated — drink at every stop and carry water on the bike
  • Ventilate your riding gear — open vents and use mesh panels
  • Don't be tempted to ride without proper gear. Skin grafts are worse than sweating.
  • Sunscreen on neck, wrists, and any exposed skin. UV radiation is intense at speed.
  • Stop more frequently — heat fatigue is real and affects concentration
July in Scotland is the sweet spot: warm enough for comfortable riding, not so hot that you overheat, and with daylight lasting until 10pm. If you're planning a Scottish tour, July delivers the best weather with acceptable midge levels.

Where to Ride in July

  • Scottish Highlands: The weather is at its best (by Highland standards). Book accommodation well in advance.
  • North England: Northumberland, the Pennines, and the Scottish Borders are less busy than the Lakes.
  • Islands: The Channel Islands, Isle of Man, Skye, Mull, and Arran are all at their best.

July Heat Management

When temperatures exceed 25°C, heat management becomes important. Dehydration causes fatigue, poor concentration, and impaired reaction times — all dangerous when riding. Carry a water bottle and drink at every stop. Electrolyte tablets or sports drinks help replace salts lost through sweating.

Your riding gear should have ventilation options for hot weather. Open vents, remove thermal liners, and consider a mesh jacket for the hottest days. But never ride without proper protection — road rash at any speed is serious, and a moment's comfort isn't worth the risk of a bare-skin crash.

Solstice Photography

The summer solstice offers unique photographic opportunities. The sun rises and sets at its most northerly points, creating unusual light angles. In Scotland, the midnight twilight — neither full dark nor full light — produces an otherworldly quality that's impossible to capture at any other time of year.

Plan your solstice route around photographic highlights. A sunrise viewpoint to start, scenic roads through the day, and a sunset location to finish creates a visual narrative of the longest day. The resulting photo series tells the story of a complete day on two wheels better than any single image.

Route Planning for Maximum Daylight

To maximise your solstice riding day, plan your route to use every minute of light. Start at a viewpoint facing east for the sunrise, ride west through the day, and finish facing west for the sunset. This natural east-to-west progression keeps the light in your favour throughout the day and creates a satisfying narrative arc from dawn to dusk.

In Scotland, the midsummer sun barely sets in the far north. Around Durness and Cape Wrath, the sky glows through the brief twilight hours, creating an eerie, beautiful light that's unique to the northern solstice. Riding through this perpetual dusk is a profound experience — the landscape takes on a dreamlike quality that you won't find at any other time of year.

Pack for temperature extremes. Predawn June temperatures can be 5-8°C, rising to 20°C+ by mid-afternoon, then dropping again in the evening. A layering system is essential. Start in full winter gear, strip down through the day, and layer up again for the sunset section. Read our UK Motorcycle Riding in August: Summer Crowds and Solutions guide for more. It is the most reliably dry month, though thunderstorms can develop on hot afternoons.
Roads are busiest as school holidays begin, so ride before 9am and midweek to beat the crowds.
Hot-weather riding demands hydration, ventilated gear, sunscreen and more frequent stops.
July is the sweet spot for Scotland: warm enough, not too hot, daylight to 10pm and acceptable midge levels.

faq.q: Is July a good month for motorcycle touring in the UK?
faq.a: July offers the most reliable weather of the year but the busiest roads. It is the warmest month on average and the most reliably dry, though thunderstorms can develop on hot afternoons and the west is wetter than the east. The trick is knowing when and where to ride, favouring early starts and midweek days to escape the school-holiday crowds.

faq.q: How do I beat the crowds in July?
faq.a: Ride early, because before 9am even popular roads are quiet and the first two hours of a July day are golden. Ride midweek, since weekend traffic in tourist areas can be three times the midweek volume. Choose less obvious destinations such as the North Pennines, Scottish Borders and mid-Wales, and use B-roads because tourist traffic sticks to A-roads.

faq.q: How should I ride safely in a July heatwave?
faq.a: When temperatures exceed 25C, heat management matters. Stay hydrated by drinking at every stop and carrying water, and consider electrolyte tablets to replace salts lost through sweating. Ventilate your gear by opening vents and removing thermal liners, but never ride without proper protection. Apply sunscreen to neck, wrists and exposed skin, and stop more frequently as heat fatigue affects concentration.

faq.q: Is July a good time to ride in Scotland?
faq.a: July is the sweet spot for Scotland: warm enough for comfortable riding but not so hot that you overheat, with daylight lasting until 10pm and acceptable midge levels. The weather is at its best by Highland standards, so book accommodation well in advance. The islands, including Skye, Mull and Arran, are also at their finest.

faq.q: Which regions are quietest in July?
faq.a: While everyone heads to the Lake District and Snowdonia, the North Pennines, Scottish Borders and mid-Wales offer comparable scenery with a fraction of the traffic. Northumberland and its coast and Cheviots are also relatively quiet. The ferry crossing filters out day-trippers, so islands like the Channel Islands, Isle of Man, Skye, Mull and Arran feel calmer than the mainland.
